clauses.normalized_text: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level request/response protocol that uses extensible semantics and self-descriptive messages for flexible interaction with network-based hypertext information systems.

clauses.normalized_text: HTTP is a generic interface protocol for information systems.
clauses.raw_text: HTTP is a generic interface protocol for information systems.

clauses.normalized_text: It is designed to hide the details of how a service is implemented by presenting a uniform interface to clients that is independent of the types of resources provided.
clauses.raw_text: It is designed to hide the details of how a service is implemented by presenting a uniform interface to clients that is independent of the types of resources provided.

clauses.normalized_text: Likewise, servers do not need to be aware of each client's purpose: an HTTP request can be considered in isolation rather than being associated with a specific type of client or a predetermined sequence of application steps.
clauses.raw_text: Likewise, servers do not need to be aware of each client's purpose: an HTTP request can be considered in isolation rather than being associated with a specific type of client or a predetermined sequence of application steps.

clauses.normalized_text: The result is a protocol that can be used effectively in many different contexts and for which implementations can evolve independently over time.
clauses.raw_text: The result is a protocol that can be used effectively in many different contexts and for which implementations can evolve independently over time.

clauses.normalized_text: HTTP is also designed for use as an intermediation protocol for translating communication to and from non-HTTP information systems.
clauses.raw_text: HTTP is also designed for use as an intermediation protocol for translating communication to and from non-HTTP information systems.

clauses.normalized_text: HTTP proxies and gateways can provide access to alternative information services by translating their diverse protocols into a hypertext format that can be viewed and manipulated by clients in the same way as HTTP services.
clauses.raw_text: HTTP proxies and gateways can provide access to alternative information services by translating their diverse protocols into a hypertext format that can be viewed and manipulated by clients in the same way as HTTP services.

clauses.normalized_text: One consequence of this flexibility is that the protocol cannot be defined in terms of what occurs behind the interface.
clauses.raw_text: One consequence of this flexibility is that the protocol cannot be defined in terms of what occurs behind the interface.

clauses.normalized_text: Instead, we are limited to defining the syntax of communication, the intent of received communication, and the expected behavior of recipients.
clauses.raw_text: Instead, we are limited to defining the syntax of communication, the intent of received communication, and the expected behavior of recipients.

clauses.normalized_text: If the communication is considered in isolation, then successful actions ought to be reflected in corresponding changes to the observable interface provided by servers.
clauses.raw_text: If the communication is considered in isolation, then successful actions ought to be reflected in corresponding changes to the observable interface provided by servers.

clauses.normalized_text: However, since multiple clients might act in parallel and perhaps at cross-purposes, we cannot require that such changes be observable beyond the scope of a single response.

clauses.normalized_text: HTTP was created for the World Wide Web (WWW) architecture and has evolved over time to support the scalability needs of a worldwide hypertext system.

clauses.normalized_text: HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol that operates by exchanging messages across a reliable transport- or session-layer "connection".
clauses.raw_text: HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol that operates by exchanging messages across a reliable transport- or session-layer "connection".

clauses.normalized_text: An HTTP "client" is a program that establishes a connection to a server for the purpose of sending one or more HTTP requests.
clauses.raw_text: An HTTP "client" is a program that establishes a connection to a server for the purpose of sending one or more HTTP requests.

clauses.normalized_text: An HTTP "server" is a program that accepts connections in order to service HTTP requests by sending HTTP responses.

clauses.normalized_text: The terms "client" and "server" refer only to the roles that these programs perform for a particular connection.

clauses.normalized_text: The same program might act as a client on some connections and a server on others.
clauses.raw_text: The same program might act as a client on some connections and a server on others.

clauses.normalized_text: The term "user agent" refers to any of the various client programs that initiate a request, including (but not limited to) browsers, spiders (web-based robots), command-line tools, custom applications, and mobile apps.
clauses.raw_text: The term "user agent" refers to any of the various client programs that initiate a request, including (but not limited to) browsers, spiders (web-based robots), command-line tools, custom applications, and mobile apps.

clauses.normalized_text: The term "origin server" refers to the program that can originate authoritative responses for a given target resource.
clauses.raw_text: The term "origin server" refers to the program that can originate authoritative responses for a given target resource.

clauses.normalized_text: When considering the design of HTTP, it is easy to fall into a trap of thinking that all user agents are general-purpose browsers and all origin servers are large public websites.

clauses.normalized_text: This specification targets conformance criteria according to the role of a participant in HTTP communication.

clauses.normalized_text: HTTP does not have specific length limitations for many of its protocol elements because the lengths that might be appropriate will vary widely, depending on the deployment context and purpose of the implementation.

clauses.normalized_text: While HTTP's core semantics don't change between protocol versions, the expression of them "on the wire" can change, and so the HTTP version number changes when incompatible changes are made to the wire format.
clauses.raw_text: While HTTP's core semantics don't change between protocol versions, the expression of them "on the wire" can change, and so the HTTP version number changes when incompatible changes are made to the wire format.

clauses.normalized_text: Additionally, HTTP allows incremental, backwards-compatible changes to be made to the protocol without changing its version through the use of defined extension points.
clauses.raw_text: Additionally, HTTP allows incremental, backwards-compatible changes to be made to the protocol without changing its version through the use of defined extension points.

clauses.normalized_text: HTTP defines a number of generic extension points that can be used to introduce capabilities to the protocol without introducing a new version, including methods (Section 8.4), status codes (Section 10.7), header and trailer fields (Section 5.7), and further extensibility points within defined fields (such as Cache-Control in Section 5.2.3 of [Caching]).

clauses.normalized_text: Additionally, specific versions of HTTP might have their own extensibility points, such as transfer-codings in HTTP/1.1 (Section 6.1 of [Messaging]) and HTTP/2 ([RFC7540]) SETTINGS or frame types.

clauses.normalized_text: Authors of specifications defining new fields are advised to choose a short but descriptive field name.

clauses.normalized_text: Short names avoid needless data transmission; descriptive names avoid confusion and "squatting" on names that might have broader uses.

clauses.normalized_text: To that end, limited-use fields (such as a header confined to a single application or use case) are encouraged to use a name that includes its name (or an abbreviation) as a prefix; for example, if the Foo Application needs a Description field, it might use "Foo-Desc"; "Description" is too generic, and "Foo-Description" is needlessly long.

clauses.normalized_text: While the field-name syntax is defined to allow any token character, in practice some implementations place limits on the characters they accept in field-names. To be interoperable, new field names SHOULD constrain themselves to alphanumeric characters, "-", and ".", and SHOULD begin with an alphanumeric character.

clauses.normalized_text: Other prefixes are sometimes used in HTTP field names; for example, "Accept-" is used in many content negotiation headers.

clauses.normalized_text: Via can be used for tracking message forwards, avoiding request loops, and identifying the protocol capabilities of senders along the request/response chain.

clauses.normalized_text: Each member of the Via field value represents a proxy or gateway that has forwarded the message.
clauses.raw_text: Each member of the Via field value represents a proxy or gateway that has forwarded the message.

clauses.normalized_text: Each intermediary appends its own information about how the message was received, such that the end result is ordered according to the sequence of forwarding recipients.
clauses.raw_text: Each intermediary appends its own information about how the message was received, such that the end result is ordered according to the sequence of forwarding recipients.

clauses.normalized_text: A proxy MUST send an appropriate Via header field, as described below, in each message that it forwards.
clauses.raw_text: A proxy MUST send an appropriate Via header field, as described below, in each message that it forwards.

clauses.normalized_text: An HTTP-to-HTTP gateway MUST send an appropriate Via header field in each inbound request message and MAY send a Via header field in forwarded response messages.
clauses.raw_text: An HTTP-to-HTTP gateway MUST send an appropriate Via header field in each inbound request message and MAY send a Via header field in forwarded response messages.

clauses.normalized_text: For each intermediary, the received-protocol indicates the protocol and protocol version used by the upstream sender of the message.
clauses.raw_text: For each intermediary, the received-protocol indicates the protocol and protocol version used by the upstream sender of the message.

clauses.normalized_text: Hence, the Via field value records the advertised protocol capabilities of the request/response chain such that they remain visible to downstream recipients; this can be useful for determining what backwards-incompatible features might be safe to use in response, or within a later request, as described in Section 4.2.

clauses.normalized_text: However, if the real host is considered to be sensitive information, a sender MAY replace it with a pseudonym.

clauses.normalized_text: For example, a request message could be sent from an HTTP/1.0 user agent to an internal proxy code-named "fred", which uses HTTP/1.1 to forward the request to a public proxy at p.example.net, which completes the request by forwarding it to the origin server at www.example.com.

clauses.normalized_text: Some intermediaries include features for transforming messages and their payloads.
clauses.raw_text: Some intermediaries include features for transforming messages and their payloads.

clauses.normalized_text: However, operational problems might occur when these transformations are applied to payloads intended for critical applications, such as medical imaging or scientific data analysis, particularly when integrity checks or digital signatures are used to ensure that the payload received is identical to the original.

clauses.normalized_text: An HTTP-to-HTTP proxy is called a "transforming proxy" if it is designed or configured to modify messages in a semantically meaningful way (i.e., modifications, beyond those required by normal HTTP processing, that change the message in a way that would be significant to the original sender or potentially significant to downstream recipients).
clauses.raw_text: An HTTP-to-HTTP proxy is called a "transforming proxy" if it is designed or configured to modify messages in a semantically meaningful way (i.e., modifications, beyond those required by normal HTTP processing, that change the message in a way that would be significant to the original sender or potentially significant to downstream recipients).

clauses.normalized_text: For example, a transforming proxy might be acting as a shared annotation server (modifying responses to include references to a local annotation database), a malware filter, a format transcoder, or a privacy filter.

clauses.raw_text: Such transformations are presumed to be desired by whichever client (or client organization) selected the proxy.

clauses.raw_text: If a proxy receives a target URI with a host name that is not a fully qualified domain name, it MAY add its own domain to the host name it received when forwarding the request.

clauses.raw_text: A proxy MUST NOT change the host name if the target URI contains a fully qualified domain name.

clauses.normalized_text: A proxy MUST NOT modify the "absolute-path" and "query" parts of the received target URI when forwarding it to the next inbound server, except as noted above to replace an empty path with "/" or "*".

clauses.normalized_text: Considering that a resource could be anything, and that the uniform interface provided by HTTP is similar to a window through which one can observe and act upon such a thing only through the communication of messages to some independent actor on the other side, an abstraction is needed to represent ("take the place of") the current or desired state of that thing in our communications.
clauses.raw_text: Considering that a resource could be anything, and that the uniform interface provided by HTTP is similar to a window through which one can observe and act upon such a thing only through the communication of messages to some independent actor on the other side, an abstraction is needed to represent ("take the place of") the current or desired state of that thing in our communications.

clauses.normalized_text: That abstraction is called a representation [REST].
clauses.raw_text: That abstraction is called a representation [REST].

clauses.normalized_text: For the purposes of HTTP, a "representation" is information that is intended to reflect a past, current, or desired state of a given resource, in a format that can be readily communicated via the protocol, and that consists of a set of representation metadata and a potentially unbounded stream of representation data.

clauses.raw_text: An origin server might be provided with, or be capable of generating, multiple representations that are each intended to reflect the current state of a target resource.

clauses.normalized_text: In such cases, some algorithm is used by the origin server to select one of those representations as most applicable to a given request, usually based on content negotiation.

clauses.normalized_text: When responses convey payload information, whether indicating a success or an error, the origin server often has different ways of representing that information; for example, in different formats, languages, or encodings.
clauses.raw_text: When responses convey payload information, whether indicating a success or an error, the origin server often has different ways of representing that information; for example, in different formats, languages, or encodings.

clauses.normalized_text: Likewise, different users or user agents might have differing capabilities, characteristics, or preferences that could influence which representation, among those available, would be best to deliver.

clauses.normalized_text: For this reason, HTTP provides mechanisms for content negotiation.

clauses.normalized_text: This specification defines three patterns of content negotiation that can be made visible within the protocol: "proactive" negotiation, where the server selects the representation based upon the user agent's stated preferences, "reactive" negotiation, where the server provides a list of representations for the user agent to choose from, and "request payload" negotiation, where the user agent selects the representation for a future request based upon the server's stated
clauses.raw_text: This specification defines three patterns of content negotiation that can be made visible within the protocol: "proactive" negotiation, where the server selects the representation based upon the user agent's stated preferences, "reactive" negotiation, where the server provides a list of representations for the user agent to choose from, and "request payload" negotiation, where the user agent selects the representation for a future request based upon the server's stated

clauses.normalized_text: preferences in past responses.
clauses.raw_text: preferences in past responses.

clauses.normalized_text: Other patterns of content negotiation include "conditional content", where the representation consists of multiple parts that are selectively rendered based on user agent parameters, "active content", where the representation contains a script that makes additional (more specific) requests based on the user agent characteristics, and "Transparent Content Negotiation" ([RFC2295]), where content selection is performed by an intermediary.
clauses.raw_text: Other patterns of content negotiation include "conditional content", where the representation consists of multiple parts that are selectively rendered based on user agent parameters, "active content", where the representation contains a script that makes additional (more specific) requests based on the user agent characteristics, and "Transparent Content Negotiation" ([RFC2295]), where content selection is performed by an intermediary.

clauses.normalized_text: These patterns are not mutually exclusive, and each has trade-offs in applicability and practicality.
clauses.raw_text: These patterns are not mutually exclusive, and each has trade-offs in applicability and practicality.

clauses.normalized_text: Note that, in all cases, HTTP is not aware of the resource semantics.
clauses.raw_text: Note that, in all cases, HTTP is not aware of the resource semantics.

clauses.normalized_text: The consistency with which an origin server responds to requests, over time and over the varying dimensions of content negotiation, and thus the "sameness" of a resource's observed representations over time, is determined entirely by whatever entity or algorithm selects or generates those responses.
clauses.raw_text: The consistency with which an origin server responds to requests, over time and over the varying dimensions of content negotiation, and thus the "sameness" of a resource's observed representations over time, is determined entirely by whatever entity or algorithm selects or generates those responses.

clauses.normalized_text: When content negotiation preferences are sent by the user agent in a request to encourage an algorithm located at the server to select the preferred representation, it is called proactive negotiation (a.k.a., server-driven negotiation).
clauses.raw_text: When content negotiation preferences are sent by the user agent in a request to encourage an algorithm located at the server to select the preferred representation, it is called proactive negotiation (a.k.a., server-driven negotiation).

clauses.normalized_text: Selection is based on the available representations for a response (the dimensions over which it might vary, such as language, content-coding, etc.) compared to various information supplied in the request, including both the explicit negotiation fields of Section 9.4 and implicit characteristics, such as the client's network address or parts of the User-Agent field.
clauses.raw_text: Selection is based on the available representations for a response (the dimensions over which it might vary, such as language, content-coding, etc.) compared to various information supplied in the request, including both the explicit negotiation fields of Section 9.4 and implicit characteristics, such as the client's network address or parts of the User-Agent field.

clauses.normalized_text: Proactive negotiation is advantageous when the algorithm for selecting from among the available representations is difficult to describe to a user agent, or when the server desires to send its "best guess" to the user agent along with the first response (hoping to avoid the round trip delay of a subsequent request if the "best guess" is good enough for the user).
clauses.raw_text: Proactive negotiation is advantageous when the algorithm for selecting from among the available representations is difficult to describe to a user agent, or when the server desires to send its "best guess" to the user agent along with the first response (hoping to avoid the round trip delay of a subsequent request if the "best guess" is good enough for the user).

clauses.normalized_text: In order to improve the server's guess, a user agent MAY send request header fields that describe its preferences.
clauses.raw_text: In order to improve the server's guess, a user agent MAY send request header fields that describe its preferences.

clauses.normalized_text: Proactive negotiation has serious disadvantages:
clauses.raw_text: Proactive negotiation has serious disadvantages:

clauses.normalized_text: o It is impossible for the server to accurately determine what might be "best" for any given user, since that would require complete knowledge of both the capabilities of the user agent and the intended use for the response (e.g., does the user want to view it on screen or print it on paper?);
clauses.raw_text: o It is impossible for the server to accurately determine what might be "best" for any given user, since that would require complete knowledge of both the capabilities of the user agent and the intended use for the response (e.g., does the user want to view it on screen or print it on paper?);

clauses.normalized_text: o Having the user agent describe its capabilities in every request can be both very inefficient (given that only a small percentage of responses have multiple representations) and a potential risk to the user's privacy;
clauses.raw_text: o Having the user agent describe its capabilities in every request can be both very inefficient (given that only a small percentage of responses have multiple representations) and a potential risk to the user's privacy;

clauses.normalized_text: o It complicates the implementation of an origin server and the algorithms for generating responses to a request; and,
clauses.raw_text: o It complicates the implementation of an origin server and the algorithms for generating responses to a request; and,

clauses.normalized_text: o It limits the reusability of responses for shared caching.

clauses.normalized_text: A user agent cannot rely on proactive negotiation preferences being consistently honored, since the origin server might not implement proactive negotiation for the requested resource or might decide that sending a response that doesn't conform to the user agent's preferences is better than sending a 406 (Not Acceptable) response.

clauses.normalized_text: With reactive negotiation (a.k.a., agent-driven negotiation), selection of the best response representation (regardless of the status code) is performed by the user agent after receiving an initial response from the origin server that contains a list of resources for alternative representations.
clauses.raw_text: With reactive negotiation (a.k.a., agent-driven negotiation), selection of the best response representation (regardless of the status code) is performed by the user agent after receiving an initial response from the origin server that contains a list of resources for alternative representations.

clauses.normalized_text: If the user agent is not satisfied by the initial response representation, it can perform a GET request on one or more of the alternative resources, selected based on metadata included in the list, to obtain a different form of representation for that response.

clauses.normalized_text: Note that the above refers to representations of the response, in general, not representations of the resource.

clauses.normalized_text: The 204 (No Content) status code indicates that the server has successfully fulfilled the request and that there is no additional content to send in the response payload body.
clauses.raw_text: The 204 (No Content) status code indicates that the server has successfully fulfilled the request and that there is no additional content to send in the response payload body.

clauses.normalized_text: Metadata in the response header fields refer to the target resource and its selected representation after the requested action was applied.
clauses.raw_text: Metadata in the response header fields refer to the target resource and its selected representation after the requested action was applied.

clauses.normalized_text: For example, if a 204 status code is received in response to a PUT request and the response contains an ETag field, then the PUT was successful and the ETag field value contains the entity-tag for the new representation of that target resource.
clauses.raw_text: For example, if a 204 status code is received in response to a PUT request and the response contains an ETag field, then the PUT was successful and the ETag field value contains the entity-tag for the new representation of that target resource.

clauses.normalized_text: The 204 response allows a server to indicate that the action has been successfully applied to the target resource, while implying that the user agent does not need to traverse away from its current "document view" (if any).
clauses.raw_text: The 204 response allows a server to indicate that the action has been successfully applied to the target resource, while implying that the user agent does not need to traverse away from its current "document view" (if any).

clauses.normalized_text: The server assumes that the user agent will provide some indication of the success to its user, in accord with its own interface, and apply any new or updated metadata in the response to its active representation.
clauses.raw_text: The server assumes that the user agent will provide some indication of the success to its user, in accord with its own interface, and apply any new or updated metadata in the response to its active representation.

clauses.normalized_text: For example, a 204 status code is commonly used with document editing interfaces corresponding to a "save" action, such that the document being saved remains available to the user for editing.
clauses.raw_text: For example, a 204 status code is commonly used with document editing interfaces corresponding to a "save" action, such that the document being saved remains available to the user for editing.

clauses.normalized_text: It is also frequently used with interfaces that expect automated data transfers to be prevalent, such as within distributed version control systems.
clauses.raw_text: It is also frequently used with interfaces that expect automated data transfers to be prevalent, such as within distributed version control systems.

clauses.normalized_text: A 204 response is terminated by the first empty line after the header fields because it cannot contain a message body.
clauses.raw_text: A 204 response is terminated by the first empty line after the header fields because it cannot contain a message body.

clauses.normalized_text: A 204 response is heuristically cacheable; i.e., unless otherwise indicated by the method definition or explicit cache controls (see Section 4.2.2 of [Caching]).
clauses.raw_text: A 204 response is heuristically cacheable; i.e., unless otherwise indicated by the method definition or explicit cache controls (see Section 4.2.2 of [Caching]).

clauses.normalized_text: The 205 (Reset Content) status code indicates that the server has fulfilled the request and desires that the user agent reset the "document view", which caused the request to be sent, to its original state as received from the origin server.
clauses.raw_text: The 205 (Reset Content) status code indicates that the server has fulfilled the request and desires that the user agent reset the "document view", which caused the request to be sent, to its original state as received from the origin server.

clauses.normalized_text: This response is intended to support a common data entry use case where the user receives content that supports data entry (a form, notepad, canvas, etc.), enters or manipulates data in that space, causes the entered data to be submitted in a request, and then the data entry mechanism is reset for the next entry so that the user can easily initiate another input action.
clauses.raw_text: This response is intended to support a common data entry use case where the user receives content that supports data entry (a form, notepad, canvas, etc.), enters or manipulates data in that space, causes the entered data to be submitted in a request, and then the data entry mechanism is reset for the next entry so that the user can easily initiate another input action.

clauses.normalized_text: Since the 205 status code implies that no additional content will be provided, a server MUST NOT generate a payload in a 205 response.
clauses.raw_text: Since the 205 status code implies that no additional content will be provided, a server MUST NOT generate a payload in a 205 response.

clauses.normalized_text: The 206 (Partial Content) status code indicates that the server is successfully fulfilling a range request for the target resource by transferring one or more parts of the selected representation.
clauses.raw_text: The 206 (Partial Content) status code indicates that the server is successfully fulfilling a range request for the target resource by transferring one or more parts of the selected representation.

clauses.normalized_text: When a 206 response is generated, the server MUST generate the following header fields, in addition to those required in the subsections below, if the field would have been sent in a 200 (OK) response to the same request: Date, Cache-Control, ETag, Expires, Content-Location, and Vary.
clauses.raw_text: When a 206 response is generated, the server MUST generate the following header fields, in addition to those required in the subsections below, if the field would have been sent in a 200 (OK) response to the same request: Date, Cache-Control, ETag, Expires, Content-Location, and Vary.

clauses.normalized_text: If a 206 is generated in response to a request with an If-Range header field, the sender SHOULD NOT generate other representation header fields beyond those required, because the client is understood to already have a prior response containing those header fields.
clauses.raw_text: If a 206 is generated in response to a request with an If-Range header field, the sender SHOULD NOT generate other representation header fields beyond those required, because the client is understood to already have a prior response containing those header fields.

clauses.normalized_text: Otherwise, the sender MUST generate all of the representation header fields that would have been sent in a 200 (OK) response to the same request.
clauses.raw_text: Otherwise, the sender MUST generate all of the representation header fields that would have been sent in a 200 (OK) response to the same request.

clauses.normalized_text: A 206 response is heuristically cacheable; i.e., unless otherwise indicated by explicit cache controls (see Section 4.2.2 of [Caching]).
clauses.raw_text: A 206 response is heuristically cacheable; i.e., unless otherwise indicated by explicit cache controls (see Section 4.2.2 of [Caching]).

clauses.normalized_text: If a single part is being transferred, the server generating the 206 response MUST generate a Content-Range header field, describing what range of the selected representation is enclosed, and a payload consisting of the range.
clauses.raw_text: If a single part is being transferred, the server generating the 206 response MUST generate a Content-Range header field, describing what range of the selected representation is enclosed, and a payload consisting of the range.

clauses.normalized_text: If multiple parts are being transferred, the server generating the 206 response MUST generate a "multipart/byteranges" payload, as defined in Section 7.3.5, and a Content-Type header field containing the multipart/byteranges media type and its required boundary parameter.
clauses.raw_text: If multiple parts are being transferred, the server generating the 206 response MUST generate a "multipart/byteranges" payload, as defined in Section 7.3.5, and a Content-Type header field containing the multipart/byteranges media type and its required boundary parameter.

clauses.normalized_text: To avoid confusion with single-part responses, a server MUST NOT generate a Content-Range header field in the HTTP header section of a multiple part response (this field will be sent in each part instead).
clauses.raw_text: To avoid confusion with single-part responses, a server MUST NOT generate a Content-Range header field in the HTTP header section of a multiple part response (this field will be sent in each part instead).

clauses.normalized_text: Within the header area of each body part in the multipart payload, the server MUST generate a Content-Range header field corresponding to the range being enclosed in that body part.
clauses.raw_text: Within the header area of each body part in the multipart payload, the server MUST generate a Content-Range header field corresponding to the range being enclosed in that body part.

clauses.normalized_text: If the selected representation would have had a Content-Type header field in a 200 (OK) response, the server SHOULD generate that same Content-Type field in the header area of each body part.
clauses.raw_text: If the selected representation would have had a Content-Type header field in a 200 (OK) response, the server SHOULD generate that same Content-Type field in the header area of each body part.

clauses.normalized_text: When multiple ranges are requested, a server MAY coalesce any of the ranges that overlap, or that are separated by a gap that is smaller than the overhead of sending multiple parts, regardless of the order in which the corresponding range-spec appeared in the received Range header field.
clauses.raw_text: When multiple ranges are requested, a server MAY coalesce any of the ranges that overlap, or that are separated by a gap that is smaller than the overhead of sending multiple parts, regardless of the order in which the corresponding range-spec appeared in the received Range header field.

clauses.normalized_text: Since the typical overhead between parts of a multipart/byteranges payload is around 80 bytes, depending on the selected representation's media type and the chosen boundary parameter length, it can be less efficient to transfer many small disjoint parts than it is to transfer the entire selected representation.
clauses.raw_text: Since the typical overhead between parts of a multipart/byteranges payload is around 80 bytes, depending on the selected representation's media type and the chosen boundary parameter length, it can be less efficient to transfer many small disjoint parts than it is to transfer the entire selected representation.

clauses.raw_text: A server MUST NOT generate a multipart response to a request for a single range, since a client that does not request multiple parts might not support multipart responses.

clauses.normalized_text: However, a server MAY generate a multipart/byteranges payload with only a single body part if multiple ranges were requested and only one range was found to be satisfiable or only one range remained after coalescing.
clauses.raw_text: However, a server MAY generate a multipart/byteranges payload with only a single body part if multiple ranges were requested and only one range was found to be satisfiable or only one range remained after coalescing.

clauses.normalized_text: A client that cannot process a multipart/byteranges response MUST NOT generate a request that asks for multiple ranges.
clauses.raw_text: A client that cannot process a multipart/byteranges response MUST NOT generate a request that asks for multiple ranges.

clauses.normalized_text: When a multipart response payload is generated, the server SHOULD send the parts in the same order that the corresponding range-spec appeared in the received Range header field, excluding those ranges that were deemed unsatisfiable or that were coalesced into other ranges.
clauses.raw_text: When a multipart response payload is generated, the server SHOULD send the parts in the same order that the corresponding range-spec appeared in the received Range header field, excluding those ranges that were deemed unsatisfiable or that were coalesced into other ranges.

clauses.normalized_text: A client that receives a multipart response MUST inspect the Content-Range header field present in each body part in order to determine which range is contained in that body part; a client cannot rely on receiving the same ranges that it requested, nor the same order that it requested.
clauses.raw_text: A client that receives a multipart response MUST inspect the Content-Range header field present in each body part in order to determine which range is contained in that body part; a client cannot rely on receiving the same ranges that it requested, nor the same order that it requested.

clauses.normalized_text: A response might transfer only a subrange of a representation if the connection closed prematurely or if the request used one or more Range specifications.
clauses.raw_text: A response might transfer only a subrange of a representation if the connection closed prematurely or if the request used one or more Range specifications.

clauses.normalized_text: After several such transfers, a client might have received several ranges of the same representation.
clauses.raw_text: After several such transfers, a client might have received several ranges of the same representation.

clauses.normalized_text: These ranges can only be safely combined if they all have in common the same strong validator (Section 11.2.1).
clauses.raw_text: These ranges can only be safely combined if they all have in common the same strong validator (Section 11.2.1).

clauses.normalized_text: A client that has received multiple partial responses to GET requests on a target resource MAY combine those responses into a larger continuous range if they share the same strong validator.
clauses.raw_text: A client that has received multiple partial responses to GET requests on a target resource MAY combine those responses into a larger continuous range if they share the same strong validator.

clauses.normalized_text: If the most recent response is an incomplete 200 (OK) response, then the header fields of that response are used for any combined response and replace those of the matching stored responses.
clauses.raw_text: If the most recent response is an incomplete 200 (OK) response, then the header fields of that response are used for any combined response and replace those of the matching stored responses.

clauses.normalized_text: If the most recent response is a 206 (Partial Content) response and at least one of the matching stored responses is a 200 (OK), then the combined response header fields consist of the most recent 200 response's header fields. If all of the matching stored responses are 206 responses, then the stored response with the most recent header fields is used as the source of header fields for the combined response, except that the client MUST use other header fields provided in the new response, aside from Content-Range, to replace all instances of the corresponding header fields in the stored response.
clauses.raw_text: If the most recent response is a 206 (Partial Content) response and at least one of the matching stored responses is a 200 (OK), then the combined response header fields consist of the most recent 200 response's header fields. If all of the matching stored responses are 206 responses, then the stored response with the most recent header fields is used as the source of header fields for the combined response, except that the client MUST use other header fields provided in the new response, aside from Content-Range, to replace all instances of the corresponding header fields in the stored response.

clauses.normalized_text: The combined response message body consists of the union of partial content ranges in the new response and each of the selected responses.
clauses.raw_text: The combined response message body consists of the union of partial content ranges in the new response and each of the selected responses.

clauses.normalized_text: If the union consists of the entire range of the representation, then the client MUST process the combined response as if it were a complete 200 (OK) response, including a Content-Length header field that reflects the complete length.
clauses.raw_text: If the union consists of the entire range of the representation, then the client MUST process the combined response as if it were a complete 200 (OK) response, including a Content-Length header field that reflects the complete length.

clauses.normalized_text: Otherwise, the client MUST process the set of continuous ranges as one of the following: an incomplete 200 (OK) response if the combined response is a prefix of the representation, a single 206 (Partial Content) response containing a multipart/byteranges body, or multiple 206 (Partial Content) responses, each with one continuous range that is indicated by a Content-Range header field.
clauses.raw_text: Otherwise, the client MUST process the set of continuous ranges as one of the following: an incomplete 200 (OK) response if the combined response is a prefix of the representation, a single 206 (Partial Content) response containing a multipart/byteranges body, or multiple 206 (Partial Content) responses, each with one continuous range that is indicated by a Content-Range header field.

clauses.normalized_text: The 3xx (Redirection) class of status code indicates that further action needs to be taken by the user agent in order to fulfill the request.
clauses.raw_text: The 3xx (Redirection) class of status code indicates that further action needs to be taken by the user agent in order to fulfill the request.

clauses.normalized_text: If a Location header field (Section 11.1.2) is provided, the user agent MAY automatically redirect its request to the URI referenced by the Location field value, even if the specific status code is not understood.
clauses.raw_text: If a Location header field (Section 11.1.2) is provided, the user agent MAY automatically redirect its request to the URI referenced by the Location field value, even if the specific status code is not understood.

clauses.normalized_text: Automatic redirection needs to be done with care for methods not known to be safe, as defined in Section 8.2.1, since the user might not wish to redirect an unsafe request.

clauses.normalized_text: There are several types of redirects:
clauses.raw_text: There are several types of redirects:

clauses.normalized_text: 1. Redirects that indicate the resource might be available at a different URI, as provided by the Location field, as in the status codes 301 (Moved Permanently), 302 (Found), 307 (Temporary Redirect), and 308 (Permanent Redirect).
clauses.raw_text: 1. Redirects that indicate the resource might be available at a different URI, as provided by the Location field, as in the status codes 301 (Moved Permanently), 302 (Found), 307 (Temporary Redirect), and 308 (Permanent Redirect).

clauses.normalized_text: 2. Redirection that offers a choice of matching resources, each capable of representing the original target resource, as in the 300 (Multiple Choices) status code.
clauses.raw_text: 2. Redirection that offers a choice of matching resources, each capable of representing the original target resource, as in the 300 (Multiple Choices) status code.

clauses.normalized_text: 3. Redirection to a different resource, identified by the Location field, that can represent an indirect response to the request, as in the 303 (See Other) status code.
clauses.raw_text: 3. Redirection to a different resource, identified by the Location field, that can represent an indirect response to the request, as in the 303 (See Other) status code.

clauses.normalized_text: 4. Redirection to a previously cached result, as in the 304 (Not Modified) status code.
clauses.raw_text: 4. Redirection to a previously cached result, as in the 304 (Not Modified) status code.

clauses.normalized_text: *Note:* In HTTP/1.0, the status codes 301 (Moved Permanently) and 302 (Found) were defined for the first type of redirect ([RFC1945], Section 9.3).
clauses.raw_text: *Note:* In HTTP/1.0, the status codes 301 (Moved Permanently) and 302 (Found) were defined for the first type of redirect ([RFC1945], Section 9.3).

clauses.raw_text: Early user agents split on whether the method applied to the redirect target would be the same as the original request or would be rewritten as GET.

clauses.normalized_text: Although HTTP originally defined the former semantics for 301 and 302 (to match its original implementation at CERN), and defined 303 (See Other) to match the latter semantics, prevailing practice gradually converged on the latter semantics for 301 and 302 as well.

clauses.normalized_text: For the same reason, 308 (Permanent Redirect) was later on added in [RFC7538] to match 301.

clauses.normalized_text: Over 10 years later, most user agents still do method rewriting for 301 and 302; therefore, [RFC7231] made that behavior conformant when the original request is POST.
clauses.raw_text: Over 10 years later, most user agents still do method rewriting for 301 and 302; therefore, [RFC7231] made that behavior conformant when the original request is POST.

clauses.normalized_text: The 300 (Multiple Choices) status code indicates that the target resource has more than one representation, each with its own more specific identifier, and information about the alternatives is being provided so that the user (or user agent) can select a preferred representation by redirecting its request to one or more of those identifiers.
clauses.raw_text: The 300 (Multiple Choices) status code indicates that the target resource has more than one representation, each with its own more specific identifier, and information about the alternatives is being provided so that the user (or user agent) can select a preferred representation by redirecting its request to one or more of those identifiers.

clauses.normalized_text: In other words, the server desires that the user agent engage in reactive negotiation to select the most appropriate representation(s) for its needs (Section 7.4).

clauses.normalized_text: The HTTP authentication framework does not define a single mechanism for maintaining the confidentiality of credentials; instead, each authentication scheme defines how the credentials are encoded prior to transmission.
clauses.raw_text: The HTTP authentication framework does not define a single mechanism for maintaining the confidentiality of credentials; instead, each authentication scheme defines how the credentials are encoded prior to transmission.

clauses.normalized_text: While this provides flexibility for the development of future authentication schemes, it is inadequate for the protection of existing schemes that provide no confidentiality on their own, or that do not sufficiently protect against replay attacks.
clauses.raw_text: While this provides flexibility for the development of future authentication schemes, it is inadequate for the protection of existing schemes that provide no confidentiality on their own, or that do not sufficiently protect against replay attacks.

clauses.normalized_text: Furthermore, if the server expects credentials that are specific to each individual user, the exchange of those credentials will have the effect of identifying that user even if the content within credentials remains confidential.
clauses.raw_text: Furthermore, if the server expects credentials that are specific to each individual user, the exchange of those credentials will have the effect of identifying that user even if the content within credentials remains confidential.

clauses.normalized_text: HTTP depends on the security properties of the underlying transport- or session-level connection to provide confidential transmission of fields.
clauses.raw_text: HTTP depends on the security properties of the underlying transport- or session-level connection to provide confidential transmission of fields.

clauses.normalized_text: In other words, if a server limits access to authenticated users using this framework, the server needs to ensure that the connection is properly secured in accordance with the nature of the authentication scheme used.
clauses.raw_text: In other words, if a server limits access to authenticated users using this framework, the server needs to ensure that the connection is properly secured in accordance with the nature of the authentication scheme used.

clauses.normalized_text: For example, services that depend on individual user authentication often require a connection to be secured with TLS ("Transport Layer Security", [RFC8446]) prior to exchanging any credentials.
clauses.raw_text: For example, services that depend on individual user authentication often require a connection to be secured with TLS ("Transport Layer Security", [RFC8446]) prior to exchanging any credentials.

clauses.normalized_text: Existing HTTP clients and user agents typically retain authentication information indefinitely.
clauses.raw_text: Existing HTTP clients and user agents typically retain authentication information indefinitely.

clauses.normalized_text: HTTP does not provide a mechanism for the origin server to direct clients to discard these cached credentials, since the protocol has no awareness of how credentials are obtained or managed by the user agent.
clauses.raw_text: HTTP does not provide a mechanism for the origin server to direct clients to discard these cached credentials, since the protocol has no awareness of how credentials are obtained or managed by the user agent.

clauses.normalized_text: The mechanisms for expiring or revoking credentials can be specified as part of an authentication scheme definition.
clauses.raw_text: The mechanisms for expiring or revoking credentials can be specified as part of an authentication scheme definition.

clauses.normalized_text: Circumstances under which credential caching can interfere with the application's security model include but are not limited to:
clauses.raw_text: Circumstances under which credential caching can interfere with the application's security model include but are not limited to:

clauses.normalized_text: o Clients that have been idle for an extended period, following which the server might wish to cause the client to re-prompt the user for credentials.
clauses.raw_text: o Clients that have been idle for an extended period, following which the server might wish to cause the client to re-prompt the user for credentials.

clauses.normalized_text: o Applications that include a session termination indication (such as a "logout" or "commit" button on a page) after which the server side of the application "knows" that there is no further reason for the client to retain the credentials.
clauses.raw_text: o Applications that include a session termination indication (such as a "logout" or "commit" button on a page) after which the server side of the application "knows" that there is no further reason for the client to retain the credentials.

clauses.normalized_text: User agents that cache credentials are encouraged to provide a readily accessible mechanism for discarding cached credentials under user control.
clauses.raw_text: User agents that cache credentials are encouraged to provide a readily accessible mechanism for discarding cached credentials under user control.

clauses.normalized_text: Authentication schemes that solely rely on the "realm" mechanism for establishing a protection space will expose credentials to all resources on an origin server.
clauses.raw_text: Authentication schemes that solely rely on the "realm" mechanism for establishing a protection space will expose credentials to all resources on an origin server.

clauses.normalized_text: Clients that have successfully made authenticated requests with a resource can use the same authentication credentials for other resources on the same origin server.
clauses.raw_text: Clients that have successfully made authenticated requests with a resource can use the same authentication credentials for other resources on the same origin server.

clauses.normalized_text: This makes it possible for a different resource to harvest authentication credentials for other resources.
clauses.raw_text: This makes it possible for a different resource to harvest authentication credentials for other resources.

clauses.normalized_text: This is of particular concern when an origin server hosts resources for multiple parties under the same canonical root URI (Section 9.5.2).
clauses.raw_text: This is of particular concern when an origin server hosts resources for multiple parties under the same canonical root URI (Section 9.5.2).

clauses.normalized_text: Possible mitigation strategies include restricting direct access to authentication credentials (i.e., not making the content of the Authorization request header field available), and separating protection spaces by using a different host name (or port number) for each party.
clauses.raw_text: Possible mitigation strategies include restricting direct access to authentication credentials (i.e., not making the content of the Authorization request header field available), and separating protection spaces by using a different host name (or port number) for each party.

clauses.normalized_text: Adding information to responses that are sent over an unencrypted channel can affect security and privacy.
clauses.raw_text: Adding information to responses that are sent over an unencrypted channel can affect security and privacy.

clauses.normalized_text: The presence of the Authentication-Info and Proxy-Authentication-Info header fields alone indicates that HTTP authentication is in use.
clauses.raw_text: The presence of the Authentication-Info and Proxy-Authentication-Info header fields alone indicates that HTTP authentication is in use.
